WebFetch response caching is documented as 15 minutes per URL but in practice returned bodies from the 2026-09-02 run when this run requested the identical /api/feed URL strings 8 days later. Five feeds appeared frozen at their 09-01/09-02 content while the upstreams, fetched directly, were current to 09-09. Appending a per-run nonce query param to the dxedge URL (for example &nonce=0910a) changes the WebFetch cache key while leaving the backend behaviour identical, because /api/feed keys its own cache on the url param alone and FastAPI ignores the extra param. EVERY nightly /api/feed and /api/* check must carry a fresh nonce, or it is testing this container's cache instead of the site. A feed that looks stale should be confirmed against the upstream before it is reported. WORSE THAN DOCUMENTED, 2026-09-18: a CHANGED cache-busting param did not defeat it. /api/health?cb=20260918run1 at 04:14Z and /api/health?cb=20260918post at 05:00Z returned byte-identical bodies carrying the same 04:14:25Z timestamp, while a python fetch at 05:00Z returned a fresh 05:00:28Z. So a distinct cb/nonce value is necessary but NOT sufficient: WebFetch can still serve a cached body for a URL it has seen before with a different query string. Practical consequence: never judge post-deploy freshness from a WebFetch timestamp alone. Confirm it against a second, independent read of the same non-denied endpoint.

The exact certificate expiry IS obtainable from this container, closing a gap every prior run recorded as unreadable. openssl and curl both see the egress proxy certificate, but the Certificate Transparency logs do not care: curl -H 'Accept: application/json' -A 'Mozilla/5.0' 'https://crt.sh/?q=dxedge.net&output=json' returns issuance and expiry for every cert ever issued for the domain. Note crt.sh returned a 502 HTML page on the first call and correct JSON on an immediate retry, so always retry once before concluding it is unavailable.

A blind WebFetch night no longer has to mean a blind cert check. The sandbox egress proxy validates the UPSTREAM certificate and fails closed: expired.badssl.com, wrong.host.badssl.com and self-signed.badssl.com all return HTTP 000 with a secure-connection error through plain curl. Therefore a curl to dxedge.net returning HTTP 200 is positive evidence that the real certificate chain is valid, even though the cert curl inspects locally is the proxy's. Run the three badssl controls each time to prove the proxy is still failing closed, then trust the result. This materially weakens awaiting_james webfetch-permission-at-setup: Steps 1, 2 and 4 are all reachable by curl, and Step 3 by the Chromium relay.

Note 433.02 MHz is 70cm, which FREQ_TO_BAND does not cover at all, so some SOTA spots would still read '?' after the unit fix.

frontend/public/crane-cab/index.html loads three.js as an ES module from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.160.0/build/three.module.js via importmap. This is the first third-party executable script on dxedge.net; every other live panel goes through the same-origin /api/feed proxy. The version is pinned and the URL is live (verified 200, 1.27 MB), so nothing is broken. The consideration is supply chain: an importmap module specifier cannot carry a subresource-integrity attribute, so a jsdelivr compromise would execute arbitrary script on the dxedge.net origin. Options: (a) leave as is, (b) vendor three.module.js into frontend/public/crane-cab/vendor/ and drop the importmap, which removes the dependency entirely, (c) keep the CDN but add a CSP script-src pinning the host. (b) is a repo change touching a page James is actively developing and (c) is an nginx.conf change, so both are his call, not autonomous repair.

awaiting_james.detail: Certificate Transparency shows four certificates issued for pay.dxedge.net and www.pay.dxedge.net by GoDaddy TLS Intermediate CA DV - R1v1, the most recent issued 2026-07-29 and valid until 2027-02-12. Neither hostname resolves: DNS returns NXDOMAIN for both, and nothing is served. dxedge.net itself resolves to 147.182.233.116, the droplet in the Mem note.
awaiting_james.assessment: Most likely benign. The timeline points at registrar auto-provisioning rather than anything hostile: on 2026-05-29, domain setup day, GoDaddy issued a cert for dxedge.net at 21:33 and for pay.dxedge.net at 21:39, and Let's Encrypt issued the droplet's own cert at 21:40. GoDaddy routinely provisions certificates for a registered domain plus product subdomains. The 2026-07-29 GoDaddy pair is a straightforward auto-renewal of that original.
awaiting_james.residual_risk: Low but not zero, and it is the kind of thing worth knowing about deliberately rather than by accident. A valid publicly-trusted DV certificate exists for a payment-suggestive name under James's domain. It is inert while no DNS record points at it, but anyone who could add or hijack that DNS record would inherit an already-trusted, already-issued cert, and a payment-themed page under a real dxedge.net name is more convincing than any lookalike domain.
awaiting_james.decision_needed: Confirm whether a GoDaddy payments or website product is intentionally enabled on the dxedge.net account. If not, cancelling that product and revoking the two GoDaddy certs removes the inert asset; CAA records on dxedge.net restricting issuance to Let's Encrypt would prevent it recurring. Both are registrar-side changes outside this routine's mandate.
